Eggs of Russian sturgeon Acipenser gueldenstaedtii incubated at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] typically hatch after 7 days , reflecting the relatively slow embryonic development characteristic of long-lived, late-maturing acipenserids. The newly emerged prolarvae carry a substantial yolk sac, and their wet weight at hatch is only 0.021 grams , a modest starting mass that underscores the reliance on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days of life. Following hatching, the transition to exogenous feeding begins relatively late compared to many teleosts; yolk-sac resorption and mouth opening occur at approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days] after fertilization under the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. First feeding typically commences between 8 and 11 days post hatch, a window during which the larvae must successfully capture suitable zooplankton prey to avoid starvation. The protracted pre-feeding interval suggests an evolutionary adaptation to uncertain food availability in the Volga-Caspian basin, where this species historically spawned, allowing larvae to survive on residual yolk while dispersing to productive foraging areas.

At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals typically measure approximately 110 centimeters [Lp = approximately 110 centimeters] in total length, marking the point at which gonadal recrudescence begins and the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes fully activated. This length threshold is reached after a prolonged juvenile phase that reflects the extremely slow life history of this species; under typical thermal conditions in the Caspian Sea basin at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], first reproduction is attained at roughly 4745 days after hatching [tR = roughly 4745 days after hatching], which translates to about 13 years. The first reproduction event, therefore, does not occur until individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic capital to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and spawning migration. This delayed maturation is consistent with what has been documented for other large-bodied Acipenseriformes and is linked to the predictability of food resources in their native estuarine and riverine habitats. Females of this species are iteroparous, returning to spawn at intervals that depend on nutritional status and environmental conditions. By deferring first reproduction until an advanced age, Russian sturgeon maximizes the probability of surviving to spawn successfully in a variable ecosystem.

The maximum recorded longevity of Acipenser gueldenstaedtii under natural conditions is 14235 days [am = 14235 days], equivalent to approximately 39 years, which places it among the more moderately long-lived members of its genus, though some congeneric species exceed 50 years at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with a slow pace of life characterized by delayed maturity, iteroparity, and considerable investment per reproductive event. Females attain an ultimate total length of 236 centimeters [Li = 236 centimeters] and can reach a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 115000 grams [Wwi = 115000 grams], representing an enormous increase from the 0.021 gram hatchling mass. Such extreme somatic growth over several decades requires a sustained high feeding rate on benthic macroinvertebrates and small fish. The species achieves this through a generalist diet and by occupying a broad trophic niche in the productive waters of the Caspian and Black Sea basins. As individuals approach senescence, growth rates slow markedly, and body condition tends to decline, though spawning may still occur in older adults if sufficient energy reserves are available.

Reproductive output in Russian sturgeon is tightly linked to female body size, with larger, older individuals contributing disproportionately to recruitment. Under optimal thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], gravid females can achieve their maximum reproductive rate, depositing eggs at a peak daily output that equates to approximately 531 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 531 eggs per day]. This high daily fecundity is sustained over the course of the spawning season, which typically lasts several weeks, meaning total seasonal fecundity can be substantial. The eggs are demersal and adhesive, attaching to gravel or rocky substrates in swift-flowing river reaches, where they undergo incubation over a period determined by temperature. Field observations indicate that once females have completed their spawning run and oviposition, they return to downstream feeding grounds to replenish depleted energy stores. The ability to produce such large numbers of eggs per spawning event reflects the evolutionary pressure to offset high rates of egg and larval mortality in the unpredictable riverine environment, where predation and flow variations can drastically reduce survival.

Comparative life-history data reveal that the total length at birth of newly hatched Russian sturgeon larvae is 1.8 centimeters [Lb = 1.8 centimeters], a size that provides a modest swimming capacity for the prolarvae to remain within suitable nursery habitats before transitioning to active feeding. In contrast, the total length at puberty of 110 centimeters [Lp = 110 centimeters] represents a sixty-fold increase in linear dimensions, emphasizing the profound morphological transformation that occurs over the first decade of life. Research on captive stocks has shown that larval growth during the first few weeks is highly sensitive to temperature, with the onset of exogenous feeding at approximately 8 to 11 days post hatch being a critical bottleneck for survival. The species' long lifespan of roughly 39 years [am = roughly 39 years] is among the longest documented for any Acipenseriformes from the Caspian basin, exceeding that of the closely related Persian sturgeon by nearly a decade and reinforcing the interpretation that Acipenser gueldenstaedtii follows a strategy of slow growth, late reproduction, and repeated spawning events at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Understanding these life-history parameters is essential for developing effective conservation and captive breeding programs, particularly as wild populations face pressures from habitat alteration and overfishing across their native range.
